reference.question: Calculate: \(5\times8\times2=?\)
reference.solution:
Method 1: Make ten from five and two

First calculate \(5\times2=10\), then multiply by 8 to get 80.

Method 2: Multiply in the written order

Multiplying in the written order gives \(5\times8=40\). Since \(4\times2=8\), doubling 40 gives 80. Thus \(5\times8\times2=80\).

nodes.description: Understand division as an unknown-factor problem. For example, find 32 ÷ 8 by finding the number that makes 32 when multiplied by 8.
nodes.label: 3.OA.B.6

nodes.description: Apply properties of operations as strategies to multiply and divide.* Examples: If 6 × 4 = 24 is known, then 4 × 6 = 24 is also known. (Commutative property of multiplication.) 3 × 5 × 2 can be found by 3 × 5 = 15, then 15 × 2 = 30, or by 5 × 2 = 10, then 3 × 10 = 30. (Associative property of multiplication.) Knowing that 8 × 5 = 40 and 8 × 2 = 16, one can find 8 × 7 as 8 × (5 + 2) = (8 × 5) + (8 × 2) = 40 + 16 = 56. (Distributive property.) *Students need not use formal terms for these properties.
nodes.label: 3.OA.B.5

The general digit-by-digit multiplication algorithm contains digit products with seven, eight and nine. Their values are required, without demanding rote recitation as the exclusive way to obtain them.

The target asks for zero-containing products and the effect of multiplying by zero, without explicitly requiring column multiplication. Place-value decomposition and distributivity compute them as well.
